analogy.p: Imagine several runners (the substances) racing along a track while a river of water (the solvent) flows in the same direction and carries them. The track is sticky in places (the paper). Runners who stick to the track more spend less time being carried by the water, so they finish short. Runners who are easily carried by the water get close to the front of the flow. The distance each runner travels compared with the distance the water travelled is the Rf value. The analogy breaks down because real substances are not trying to move: they are continuously dissolving into the solvent and being held by the paper, and the balance between the two decides how far they go.
analogy.t: A race along a sticky track

bullets: Purpose 1: **separate** the different substances in a mixture.
Purpose 2: help to **identify** substances by comparing with known substances or Rf values.
Purpose 3: test **purity**: a pure compound gives a single spot.
Typical samples: inks, dyes, food colourings, plant pigments (coloured so the spots can be seen).
Formulations such as inks and colourings can be analysed to find out which dyes they contain.
The result on the paper is called a **chromatogram**.
Colourless substances can still be separated but need to be made visible, e.g. by a locating agent or UV light (beyond the core spec).
core.p: **Chromatography** is a technique used to **separate the substances in a mixture** and to give information that helps to **identify** them. In GCSE chemistry the usual version is paper chromatography, used on coloured substances such as inks, dyes and food colourings. A small spot of the mixture is placed near the bottom of a piece of chromatography paper, which is then stood in a solvent. The solvent soaks up the paper and carries the substances in the spot with it, but different substances travel different distances, so they end up as separate spots. It is used because it needs only tiny samples and is fast, simple and cheap.

bullets: **Stationary phase** = the phase that does not move (the chromatography paper).
**Mobile phase** = the phase that moves (the solvent, e.g. water or ethanol).
Separation depends on the **distribution of substances between the two phases**: how strongly each is held by the stationary phase compared with how soluble it is in the mobile phase.
A substance that is **more soluble in the solvent** (and less attracted to the paper) moves further up the paper.
A substance that is **more strongly attracted to the paper** moves a shorter distance.
The solvent rises up the paper by capillary action as the paper soaks it up.
Different substances therefore move at different speeds and separate into different spots.
core.p: Every type of chromatography has two phases. The **stationary phase** is the one that does not move: in paper chromatography it is the paper (the cellulose fibres and water trapped in them). The **mobile phase** is the one that moves through the stationary phase: it is the **solvent**, which flows up the paper by capillary action carrying the substances with it. The separation happens because each substance is attracted differently to the two phases, so it spends a different proportion of time dissolved in the moving solvent compared with being held by the paper.

bullets: Step 1: draw a **pencil** line about 1 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper (the origin / baseline). Pencil is used because it is insoluble and will not run with the solvent; ink would dissolve and separate.

Step 2: use a capillary tube or fine pipette to place a **small spot** of each sample on the line, spaced apart, and label each lightly in pencil; add known reference substances if you want to identify components.
Step 3: pour a small amount of solvent into a beaker so that the depth is **below the pencil line** (about 0.5 to 1 cm).

Step 4: stand the paper in the beaker, with the bottom edge in the solvent but the **origin line above the solvent**, and cover with a lid or cling film to stop the solvent evaporating and keep the atmosphere saturated.
Step 5: leave it while the solvent soaks up the paper; **remove the paper before the solvent reaches the top** and immediately mark the **solvent front** in pencil, because it evaporates.
Step 6: allow the paper to dry (a flammable solvent such as ethanol is dried away from flames).
Step 7: measure the distances moved by the solvent and by each spot and calculate the Rf values.
core.h: Required practical: the method step by step
core.p: The required practical is to investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances (for example food colourings or felt-tip inks). Examiners expect you to know the method in the right order and to explain why each step matters. The same safe, repeatable procedure gives results that can be compared fairly.

bullets: Pencil line, not pen: pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent, so it does not move up the paper and create extra spots.
Origin line above the solvent level: otherwise the samples wash into the solvent instead of being carried up the paper.
Small, concentrated spots: large spots would make the separated spots overlap, so substances could not be told apart.
Lid on the beaker: stops solvent evaporating from the paper and keeps conditions consistent.
Remove before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front immediately: so that the distance moved by the solvent can be measured accurately.
Paper must not touch the sides of the beaker: otherwise the solvent front rises unevenly.
Measure to the **centre** of each spot, using the same starting line (origin) each time.
core.h: Why each step of the method matters
core.p: Mark schemes often ask why something is done. The key reasons relate to getting clear, reproducible separation and to avoiding errors. If the origin line is under the solvent the samples dissolve into the beaker and nothing travels up the paper. If the spot is too large the separate substances overlap, so the spots must be small. Using pencil prevents the line from dissolving and contaminating the result.

bullets: Water is often used for water-soluble ink and food colouring.
If a substance does not dissolve in water (e.g. permanent ink), an alternative solvent such as **ethanol** can be used.
A substance that is **insoluble** in the solvent stays at the origin (it cannot be carried up).
A very soluble substance moves close to the solvent front.
Different compounds can have different Rf values in **different solvents**, so a second solvent can separate substances that overlap in the first.
Ethanol is flammable, so keep it away from naked flames and use it in a well ventilated place.
core.p: The solvent chosen affects the result because the substances' solubility depends on the solvent. Water is used for water-soluble dyes. Some substances do not dissolve in water (for example the dyes in permanent marker pens), so another solvent, such as ethanol, must be used. A substance that cannot dissolve in the chosen solvent stays on the origin line, so a different solvent should be tried. It is the combination of paper and solvent that decides how far each substance moves.

bullets: One spot = pure (in that solvent).
Two or more spots = a mixture; count the spots to say how many substances are present.
To be sure a substance is pure, run it in more than one solvent: a pure compound gives one spot in all of them.
If a single spot appears in one solvent but two in another, the sample is a mixture whose substances only separated in the second solvent.
Spots at the **same height** (same distance) in the same solvent and paper are probably the same substance.
Spots at different heights are different substances.
Compare the chromatogram of the unknown with those of known reference substances run on the same paper at the same time.
core.h: Reading a chromatogram: pure substances and mixtures
core.p: A chromatogram can show quickly whether a sample is pure. A **pure compound** produces a **single spot** in all solvents because there is only one substance to separate. A **mixture** produces two or more spots because it contains two or more substances. The number of spots is therefore the number of (visible) substances. If a spot stays on the origin line, that substance did not dissolve in the solvent used.

bullets: Draw a horizontal line across the chromatogram through a reference spot; if the unknown's spot lies on the line it matches.
A spot that does not match any reference is an unidentified substance.
Matching spots must be from the same solvent and paper, run at the same time.
All the substances found in a mixture are listed by naming those that match known references.
This is used in forensic work (ink or fibre dyes), food testing for illegal dyes, and checking the purity of medicines.
If a mixture has more spots than references, say it contains at least the matching ones plus others not identified.
core.p: To identify the components of a mixture you can run known substances next to the unknown on the same piece of paper. If a spot from the mixture travels exactly the same distance as a reference spot, it is probably the same substance. For example, if an unknown ink gives three spots and two of them line up with dye P and dye Q, then the ink contains P and Q and a third substance that did not match either. This is a common exam setting for food colouring and ink questions.

bullets: **Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent** (both measured from the origin line).
Rearranged: distance moved by substance = Rf × distance moved by solvent.
Rearranged: distance moved by solvent = distance moved by substance ÷ Rf.
Rf has **no units** (a ratio of two distances in the same units) and is always less than 1.
Measure the substance's distance from the origin line to the **centre** of the spot; the solvent's distance from the origin line to the **solvent front**.
Both distances must be in the same units (e.g. both in mm or both in cm).
Rf values are usually given to 2 decimal places, as are most answers in exam questions.
core.p: The **Rf value** (retention factor) is a number that describes how far a substance has moved relative to the solvent. It is the ratio of the distance moved by the substance to the distance moved by the solvent. Because it is a ratio of two lengths the units cancel, so an Rf has **no units**. The substance cannot travel further than the solvent, so Rf is always **between 0 and 1** (it is a decimal, never greater than 1).

bullets: Same compound + same solvent + same paper = same Rf value every time.
Compare the calculated Rf with a table of Rf values for known compounds in that solvent to identify the compound.
Different solvents give different Rf values for the same compound.
Two different compounds can have equal Rf in one solvent; they may separate in a second solvent.
A higher Rf means the substance is more soluble in the solvent (and less attracted to the paper) than one with a lower Rf.
Rf = 0 means the substance did not move; Rf close to 1 means it travelled almost with the solvent front.
core.p: A compound has a characteristic Rf value in a given solvent. Because **different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents**, the Rf value measured from a chromatogram can be compared with Rf values in a data table to help identify an unknown compound. This works only if the same solvent (and type of paper) is used, since changing the solvent changes the Rf. If two compounds have the same Rf in one solvent they can often be separated by using another solvent, which is why using more than one solvent is good practice.

bullets: Step 1: measure the distance from the origin to the **centre** of the spot.
Step 2: measure the distance from the origin to the **solvent front**.
Step 3: write Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance.
Step 4: substitute and calculate; keep the answer between 0 and 1.
Step 5: do not add units, and give 2 decimal places (or follow the question).
Check: if you get a value above 1, you have the fraction upside down.
If given Rf and the solvent distance, find the spot distance by multiplying.
core.h: Worked method for calculating Rf (exam skill)
core.p: Rf questions are worth 2 to 3 marks and are easy marks if you are systematic. Always read the distances from the origin line, not the bottom edge of the paper. Check that both distances use the same units. Write the formula, substitute the numbers, then give the answer to the correct number of decimal places with no units. If the question gives the paper as a diagram, measure carefully with a ruler.

bullets: Substances that are not soluble in the solvent will not move; another solvent must be used.
If the solvent front is allowed to reach the top edge, the solvent distance cannot be measured correctly.
If two substances have similar Rf in a solvent, the spots overlap: use another solvent.
Link: a pure substance has a single spot (and a sharp melting point).
Link: formulations such as ink are mixtures of dyes that chromatography reveals.
Link to other separation methods: filtration, crystallisation and distillation separate by other properties; chromatography separates by differing distribution between phases.
Instrumental methods (e.g. gas chromatography) use the same principle but are faster, more sensitive and more accurate.
core.h: Limitations and links to other topics
core.p: Paper chromatography has limitations: spots of colourless substances are invisible without extra treatment, very similar substances may overlap, and results depend on the solvent and conditions, so comparisons must be made under identical conditions. Chromatography links to purity (single spot = pure), to formulations (analysing inks and food colourings), to the idea of solubility, and to the instrumental methods for analysis such as gas chromatography, which is the same principle with a gas as the mobile phase.

exam: State: stationary phase = paper (does not move); mobile phase = solvent (moves). Learn these as 1 mark answers.
Formula for Rf must be written: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. Show substitution for method marks.
Calculation answers: give 2 decimal places, no units, and check the value is between 0 and 1.
'Why use pencil?' Answer: pencil is insoluble in the solvent so does not move up the paper (ink would run and separate).
'Why must the origin line be above the solvent?' Answer: otherwise the samples dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of travelling up the paper.
For a 4 or 6 mark method question, give the steps in order: pencil line, spots, solvent below line, lid, remove before front reaches top and mark front, dry, measure, calculate Rf.
'Explain how the chromatogram shows the ink is a mixture': it has more than one spot (e.g. 3 spots), so contains at least three substances.
To identify: compare spots with references at the same height, or compare Rf with data-table values, in the same solvent.
To say a compound is pure: it gives one spot in all (several) solvents.
Explain separation with the phases: substances differ in how soluble they are in the solvent and how strongly the paper holds them, so move different distances.
If the question says a substance does not dissolve in water, suggest another solvent such as ethanol.
Measure to the centre of each spot using a ruler; both distances must have the same units.

mistakes.r: It must be in pencil because pencil does not dissolve in the solvent; ink would separate and move.
mistakes.w: The line at the bottom is drawn in pen.

mistakes.r: The solvent must be below the origin line so the samples are carried up the paper, not dissolved into the beaker.
mistakes.w: The solvent level is above the origin line.

mistakes.r: Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent (so it is never above 1).
mistakes.w: Rf = distance of solvent ÷ distance of substance.

mistakes.r: Rf is a ratio of two distances so it has no units.
mistakes.w: Giving Rf a unit such as cm or mm.

mistakes.r: Measure both distances from the origin line; spot distance to the centre of the spot.
mistakes.w: Measuring from the bottom of the paper.

mistakes.r: The paper is the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase.
mistakes.w: The paper is the mobile phase.

mistakes.r: One spot in one solvent suggests purity; a pure compound gives a single spot in all solvents.
mistakes.w: One spot proves the substance is pure.

mistakes.r: Separation depends on the distribution between phases: how soluble in the solvent compared with attraction to the paper.
mistakes.w: Substances move because they are heavier or lighter.

summary: You must know that chromatography separates the substances in a mixture and helps to identify them, using a stationary phase (paper) and a mobile phase (solvent), and that separation depends on the distribution of substances between the two phases. You must calculate Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent, know that a pure compound gives one spot in all solvents, and be able to describe the paper chromatography required practical.

terms.d: A technique used to separate the substances in a mixture and to give information to help identify them.
The phase that does not move in chromatography; in paper chromatography it is the paper.
The phase that moves in chromatography; in paper chromatography it is the solvent.
The liquid that moves up the paper and carries the substances with it.
The furthest point reached by the solvent on the chromatography paper.
The pencil line on the paper on which the sample spots are placed at the start.
The paper, with its separated spots, produced by chromatography.
The ratio of the distance moved by a compound to the distance moved by the solvent.
How a substance is shared between the mobile phase and the stationary phase; it decides how far it moves.
A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance; gives one spot in chromatography.
Two or more substances not chemically joined; gives two or more spots.
Able to dissolve in a given solvent.
A known substance run on the same chromatogram for comparison.
The movement of a liquid up a narrow space such as paper fibres, which draws the solvent up the paper.
A mixture designed as a useful product with components in measured quantities; e.g. inks and food colourings.

worked.q: In a chromatography experiment the solvent front moved 9.0 cm from the origin. A spot moved 4.5 cm. Calculate the Rf value. (2 marks)
steps: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent

worked.ans: 5.0 cm from the origin line (to the centre of the spot).
worked.q: A dye has an Rf of 0.40 in ethanol. In an experiment the solvent front moved 12.5 cm. How far did the dye spot move? (2 marks)
steps: Rearrange: distance moved by substance = Rf × distance moved by solvent

worked.ans: The colouring is a mixture of at least three substances. Two are probably E102 and E133 because they travelled the same distance as the reference dyes under the same conditions; the third is a different, unidentified substance. A second solvent would test the identification.
worked.q: A food colouring gives three spots on a chromatogram. Two of the spots are at the same height as spots from known dyes E102 and E133. Describe what this shows about the colouring and how to be more certain of the identification. (4 marks)
steps: Three spots means three substances: it is a mixture, not a pure substance.
Two spots match the known dyes at the same height, so the colouring probably contains E102 and E133.
The third spot does not match either reference so is another substance.
To be more certain, repeat using a different solvent: matching Rf values in both solvents give more reliable identification.
